<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Background: what the fork check was for

`checkpoint_remote` is normally committed in `.entire/settings.json`, so anyone who forks a project inherits it. `e8b589835` added "fork detection" to stop a contributor's session data being pushed into the upstream project's checkpoint repo — one they typically can't write to and shouldn't be writing to. Sound guard.

It was implemented by comparing **the push remote's** owner to the checkpoint repo's owner.

## The problem

That conflates two different questions: *"is this `checkpoint_remote` mine?"* and *"where is this particular push going?"* Two consequences:

- **Pushing to any differently-owned remote disables your own `checkpoint_remote`** — and the fallback then sends the checkpoints *to that remote*. A backup remote in another org, or a colleague's fork, receives your session transcripts instead of your configured checkpoint repo. Exactly the opposite of what the explicit setting asked for.
- **It cannot be expressed at all for a remote with several push URLs.** git allows `remote.<name>.pushurl` to repeat and pushes to all of them, so one boolean verdict has to cover a set of destinations that may have different owners.

Nothing in the suite pinned the intended reading: 16 of 18 `TestPushURL` cases use `pushRemote: "origin"`, and the two `"upstream"` cases exercise a *missing* remote rather than a differently-owned one. "Push remote owner" and "origin owner" were indistinguishable everywhere.

## The fix

Ask the ownership question directly, from two local signals — no network, so the pre-push path stays free of SSH passphrase/security-key prompts:

1. A `checkpoint_remote` in `.entire/settings.local.json` is gitignored and per-clone, so it **cannot** have been inherited by cloning or forking. Always ours.
2. Otherwise compare the checkpoint repo's owner against **origin's** owner: *"am I working in a repo owned by whoever owns the checkpoint repo?"* A fork clone has origin `<fork>/app` against an upstream-owned checkpoint repo, and mismatches.

The push destination no longer enters the decision, which is what makes the multi-push-URL case expressible at all.

**Both existing fork tests pass unchanged** — they were written with `originURL` set to the fork (`https://github.com/fork/app.git`, `entire://.../gh/fork/app`), which is good evidence this is the reading that was intended all along.

Signal 1 doubles as the escape hatch for a checkpoint repo legitimately owned by a different account or org than origin — a config the previous check had no way to express.

3. If there is **no origin at all**, the push remote's URL is the only identity the repo has, so it is used instead — which is what the predecessor effectively did. A repo whose only remote is e.g. `upstream` must not lose its configured checkpoint remote just because nothing is named `origin`. In that topology there is no origin-vs-push-remote divergence to worry about: the repo has exactly one identity. (Added in the second commit, from an Entire trail finding — see below.)

### What gets compared, case by case

| Scenario | Identity used | `checkpoint_remote` | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Normal repo | origin `acme/app` | `acme/checkpoints` | owners match → **honored** |
| Fork contributor, inherited committed setting | origin `fork/app` | `acme/checkpoints` | mismatch → **ignored**; checkpoints go to their own fork |
| Cross-org, set in `settings.local.json` | — (provenance short-circuit) | `myorg/checkpoints` | local-only → **honored** |
| Cross-org, committed in `settings.json` | origin `me/app` | `myorg/checkpoints` | mismatch → **ignored** — known limitation, use `settings.local.json` |
| Pushing to a `backup` remote in another org | origin `acme/app` | `acme/checkpoints` | origin decides → **honored** ← the misroute this PR fixes |
| No origin; only `upstream` = `acme/app` | push remote `acme/app` | `acme/checkpoints` | match → **honored** ← the trail-finding fix |
| Local-path origin `/tmp/repo` | unparseable | `acme/checkpoints` | owner undeterminable → **ignored** (prior behavior preserved) |

The property that matters: the last three rows no longer depend on *where this particular push is headed*, which is what makes the multi-push-URL case expressible at all.

## Also in here

- **Read the push remote's URL with `git remote get-url --push`** when deriving transport. A remote's push destination is `remote.<name>.pushurl` when set, so the plain `url` can name a different repository than the one being pushed to. Latent until now because `url == pushurl` in the common case.
- **The inherited case logs at Warn instead of Debug**, with the `settings.local.json` hint, so a user whose `checkpoint_remote` is being ignored can find out why.

## Behavior changes

| Scenario | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Fork clone, inherited committed setting | ignored, checkpoints → your remote | unchanged |
| Own repo, push to a differently-owned remote | **ignored, checkpoints → that remote** | honored, checkpoints → checkpoint repo |
| `checkpoint_remote` in `settings.local.json`, origin owner differs | ignored | honored |
| Remote with a `pushurl` in another repo | transport from the fetch url | transport from the push url |
| Origin absent, same-owner push remote | honored (push-remote owner) | honored (push-remote owner) |
| Non-forge URL, e.g. a local path (owner undeterminable) | fallback | unchanged |

## Second commit: Entire trail finding (trail 971, medium)

The review agent caught that the first commit regressed one topology: keying ownership on origin made a **missing** origin read as "inherited", so a repo whose only remote is `upstream` — with an owner matching the checkpoint repo — silently lost checkpoint-remote routing, where the predecessor would have used it. Origin still decides when it exists; only its complete absence falls back to the push remote as identity. The check moved after the push-remote read (needed for transport anyway) to have that URL available, and the reason strings now name which remote was consulted.

Finding resolved on the trail with the fixing commit.

## Not in scope

Divergence recovery across multiple push URLs is a separate problem with its own constraint (fast-forward-only push plus one local ref cannot satisfy N independently diverged remotes with cherry-pick reconciliation). It's documented with executable specs in #1897 and needs its own design.

## Test plan

- Three new `TestPushURL` cases, each verified to fail against the previous implementation: differently-owned push remote with matching origin; `settings.local.json` provenance; transport derived from the push URL. ## Background: what the fork check was for

`checkpoint_remote` is normally committed in `.entire/settings.json`, so anyone who forks a project inherits it. `e8b589835` added "fork detection" to stop a contributor's session data being pushed into the upstream project's checkpoint repo — one they typically can't write to and shouldn't be writing to. Sound guard.

It was implemented by comparing **the push remote's** owner to the checkpoint repo's owner.

## The problem

That conflates two different questions: *"is this `checkpoint_remote` mine?"* and *"where is this particular push going?"* Two consequences:

- **Pushing to any differently-owned remote disables your own `checkpoint_remote`** — and the fallback then sends the checkpoints *to that remote*. A backup remote in another org, or a colleague's fork, receives your session transcripts instead of your configured checkpoint repo. Exactly the opposite of what the explicit setting asked for.
- **It cannot be expressed at all for a remote with several push URLs.** git allows `remote.<name>.pushurl` to repeat and pushes to all of them, so one boolean verdict has to cover a set of destinations that may have different owners.

Nothing in the suite pinned the intended reading: 16 of 18 `TestPushURL` cases use `pushRemote: "origin"`, and the two `"upstream"` cases exercise a *missing* remote rather than a differently-owned one. "Push remote owner" and "origin owner" were indistinguishable everywhere.

Ask the ownership question directly, from two local signals — no network, so the pre-push path stays free of SSH passphrase/security-key prompts:

1. A `checkpoint_remote` in `.entire/settings.local.json` is gitignored and per-clone, so it **cannot** have been inherited by cloning or forking. Always ours.
2. Otherwise compare the checkpoint repo's owner against **origin's** owner: *"am I working in a repo owned by whoever owns the checkpoint repo?"* A fork clone has origin `<fork>/app` against an upstream-owned checkpoint repo, and mismatches.

The push destination no longer enters the decision, which is what makes the multi-push-URL case expressible at all.

**Both existing fork tests pass unchanged** — they were written with `originURL` set to the fork (`https://github.com/fork/app.git`, `entire://.../gh/fork/app`), which is good evidence this is the reading that was intended all along.

Signal 1 doubles as the escape hatch for a checkpoint repo legitimately owned by a different account or org than origin — a config the previous check had no way to express.

3. If there is **no origin at all**, the push remote's URL is the only identity the repo has, so it is used instead — which is what the predecessor effectively did. A repo whose only remote is e.g. `upstream` must not lose its configured checkpoint remote just because nothing is named `origin`. | Fork contributor, inherited committed setting | origin `fork/app` | `acme/checkpoints` | mismatch → **ignored**; checkpoints go to their own fork |
| Cross-org, set in `settings.local.json` | — (provenance short-circuit) | `myorg/checkpoints` | local-only → **honored** |
| Cross-org, committed in `settings.json` | origin `me/app` | `myorg/checkpoints` | mismatch → **ignored** — known limitation, use `settings.local.json` |
| Pushing to a `backup` remote in another org | origin `acme/app` | `acme/checkpoints` | origin decides → **honored** ← the misroute this PR fixes |
| No origin; only `upstream` = `acme/app` | push remote `acme/app` | `acme/checkpoints` | match → **honored** ← the trail-finding fix |
| Local-path origin `/tmp/repo` | unparseable | `acme/checkpoints` | owner undeterminable → **ignored** (prior behavior preserved) |

The property that matters: the last three rows no longer depend on *where this particular push is headed*, which is what makes the multi-push-URL case expressible at all.

|---|---|---|

## Why refs need one destination

The push-discovery queue records only a ref — `{"ref": …}`, no per-destination state — so *"this ref is pushed"* has to mean one place. git's fan-out across a remote's several push URLs can't provide that, in two distinct ways:

1. **One failing URL fails the whole invocation**, so no ref unqueues even though other URLs took it. A dead mirror wedges the queue indefinitely, retried on every push.
2. **git's iteration isn't uniform.** A ref *rejection* returns and git carries on to later URLs; a *transport* failure (missing repo, auth, bad host) `die()`s. Verified:

| First URL fails with… | Later URLs | Exit |
|---|---|---|
| non-fast-forward rejection | ✅ still pushed | 1 |
| unreachable / transport | ❌ **skipped entirely** | 128 |

So an unreachable mirror in *first* position meant nothing was pushed anywhere, while the same mirror last was harmless. Position silently decided the outcome.

## What changes

When a remote carries **more than one push URL**, checkpoint refs target its **first push URL** directly and the rest are skipped. The recovery fetch uses the same target, which also fixes a real mismatch: fan-out reconciled the remote's *fetch* url while pushing to its pushurls, so with a `pushurl` configured we were reconciling a repository nothing had been pushed to.

**A single push URL keeps the remote NAME as the target**, so the overwhelmingly common topology is byte-identical to before — remote-tracking refs still update, output still says `origin`, no URL-keyed promisor config appears. Only multi-URL remotes are affected.

**git-branch deliberately keeps fan-out.** Its v1 branch is a single shared ref with no queue to keep coherent, and mirroring it to every push URL is what people configure those remotes for (guarded by `..._Branch_RepeatedPushesKeepBothURLsInSync` in #1897). The backends therefore differ on multi-URL remotes; that's documented at the decision point in `refs_push_destination.go` rather than left to be discovered.

### Trade, accepted deliberately

- Checkpoint refs live in **exactly one repository**. Clone that repository and reads resolve (its url becomes the clone's fetch URL); clone a different mirror of the same code and they don't. `checkpoint_remote` remains the way to name a checkpoint repository explicitly.
- A first push URL that **rejects** a ref no longer lets later URLs receive it. git would have carried on; we stop. That's the price of a destination the queue can reason about.

## Saying where — three surfaces

Since the choice is otherwise invisible:

- **pre-push** warns on stderr, naming the chosen URL and how many were skipped;
- **`entire enable`** notes it (both the first-time setup path and re-enable);
- **`entire doctor`** reports it under `Checkpoint destination: REVIEW`.

All three also cover the *other* ambiguous topology — **several remotes**, where checkpoints follow whichever remote you push to while `resume`/`explain` always read via `origin`, so checkpoints pushed elsewhere aren't found again. All are silent on an ordinary repo and whenever `checkpoint_remote` already pins a destination.

- The batch-rejection retry claimed **"Some checkpoint refs diverged"** for *every* failure, including an unreachable destination — pointing users at the wrong problem. It now says the push was rejected without asserting why.
- `printCheckpointRemoteHint` ("a checkpoint remote is configured in Entire settings") fired for any URL target, and would now fire for a URL we picked ourselves. Gated on an actual `checkpoint_remote`.
- `RedactURL` renders a plain filesystem path as `:///path/to/repo`; display now passes paths through and only redacts URL-shaped values.

+		}

+type refsPushDestination struct {
+	// target is passed to git push and to the recovery fetch: a remote name, or a URL.
+	target string

+	// checkpoint_remote. It cannot be recovered from target's shape — a
+	// resolved push URL is URL-shaped too — and it decides both how the
+	// destination is named and whether the "a checkpoint remote is configured"
+	// hint applies.

+	// receive checkpoint refs. Zero in every single-destination topology.
+	ignoredPushURLs int

+//     URLs receive it. git would have carried on to them; we stop. That is the

+	)

I've read all three diffs. Here's the interaction picture.

## The three PRs answer three layers of one question

| | Question | Resolver | Signal |
|---|---|---|---|
| **#1893** | *Which remote* may carry checkpoints? | `strategy.ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote` | `checkpoint_push_remote` → branch push destination → `origin` → sole → first |
| **#1898** | Is the configured `checkpoint_remote` *mine*? | `remote.checkpointRemoteIsInherited` | `settings.local.json` provenance → **origin's** owner |
| **#1905** | *Which push URL* of that remote gets the refs? | `strategy.resolveRefsPushDestination` | first push URL when >1 |

Order-wise they compose cleanly: #1893's gate sits after `resolvePushSettings` (which runs #1898's logic) and before `prePushCheckpointRefs` (which runs #1905's). No structural fight. The problems are semantic.

## 1. #1893's tracking tier + #1898's origin-keyed ownership regress the fork guard

#1893's second precedence tier exists explicitly for *"cloned base + added fork"* — origin is the upstream you can't push, the branch tracks your fork. #1898 decides `checkpoint_remote` ownership by comparing the checkpoint repo's owner to **origin's** owner.

In exactly that topology those two disagree about what "mine" means:

- origin = `acme/app` (upstream), committed `checkpoint_remote: acme/checkpoints`, you push to `myfork`
- #1898: origin owner `acme` == checkpoint owner `acme` → **not inherited → honored**
- #1893's gate exempts `hasCheckpointURL()`, so it doesn't intervene

A contributor's session transcripts now target the upstream project's checkpoint repo — the precise thing `e8b589835` was added to prevent. Usual outcome is an auth failure and checkpoints never leaving the machine (with a fail-soft warning every push); where the contributor does have write access, they land upstream. Pre-#1898 behavior: push remote owner `myfork` ≠ `acme` → fallback → checkpoints to the fork, which worked.

#1898's own table only covers fork-clone (`origin = fork/app`). This is the same class as the regression its second commit already fixed from the trail finding — *keying on origin assumes origin is yours* — and #1893 is the PR that argues that assumption is wrong often enough to need a whole precedence tier.

## 2. #1893's tracking tier makes reads unrecoverable, and #1905 is the PR that says so

Read paths hardcode `origin` remote-tracking refs — `strategy/common.go:551,1069,1609`, `checkpoint/persistent.go:2198`, `metadata_reconcile.go:82`. #1893's body acknowledges this ("Read paths still target `origin` (coherent with the default election)"), but that coherence holds only for the `default`/`sole` tiers. With `tracking` winning, the elected remote is by construction allowed to differ from origin — and the gate then *blocks* the push to origin that used to make reads work. In the fork topology, before #1893 pushing to origin synced checkpoints there and `resume` found them; after #1893 nothing ever reaches origin, so reads never resolve.

#1905's `remote_topology.go` spells out this exact failure mode as a warning worth printing:

> Checkpoints follow whichever remote you push to, while reading them back (resume, explain) always looks at origin — so checkpoints pushed elsewhere are not found again from this clone.

So #1893 systematizes the condition #1905 warns about, while #1905's wording becomes wrong once #1893 lands (checkpoints no longer follow whichever remote you push to — one is elected). My read: the read-side follow-up (#1634) stops being optional if the tracking tier ships. Either land the read-side resolver first, or drop the tracking tier from #1893 and let `checkpoint_push_remote` serve that topology — it's the one tier that can point checkpoints somewhere reads can't see.

## 3. #1893 and #1898 fix overlapping halves of the same bug

#1898's headline case — *"pushing to a `backup` remote in another org sends your transcripts there"* — cannot happen at all once #1893's gate lands: the push to `backup` carries no checkpoint work. #1898 remains load-bearing for the cases where the differently-owned remote **is** the elected one (sole remote, or the branch's push destination), plus the `pushurl` transport fix and the `settings.local.json` escape hatch. Worth stating in whichever lands second, so the next reader doesn't conclude one of them is redundant.

## 4. Three settings, two destination surfaces, three enumerations

- **Settings:** `checkpoint_push_remote` (#1893, remote name), `checkpoint_remote` (#1898 ownership), implicit first-push-URL (#1905). #1905's advice line — *"To pin one repository for checkpoints, set `checkpoint_remote`"* — should mention `checkpoint_push_remote` for the multi-remote case after #1893.
- **Surfaces:** #1893 adds `entire status` "Checkpoints sync to: origin"; #1905 adds the `enable`/`doctor` topology note. They use different resolvers, so status can name a remote whose refs actually go to one specific URL of it. Compose them: status should report the elected remote *and* the resolved URL.
- **Enumerations:** #1893's `configuredRemotesInConfigOrder` shells `git config --local --get-regexp` (misses non-local/included config, pushurl-only remotes deliberately invisible); #1905's `pushURLsByRemote` parses `git remote -v`. One helper, please.

Two comments in #1905 go stale under #1898: `remoteDestination.pinned`'s rationale ("PushURL falls back to the push remote on an owner mismatch") — after #1898 the mismatch is origin-keyed, so `pinned` is near-constant across remotes and the per-remote probe loop is redundant. And #1905's `remote.IsURL(target)` branch becomes unreachable from pre-push once #1893 gates raw-URL pushes; only the migrate path reaches it.

## 5. Mechanical

- **#1898 ↔ #1905:** both add `gitremote.GetPushURLs` (identical), and both insert into `checkpoint/remote/util.go` immediately after `GetRemoteURL` → guaranteed conflict, trivial. #1898's `remote.GetPushURL` should become `GetPushURLs(...)[0]`.
- **#1893 ↔ #1898:** `settings/settings.go` at ~1420 and ~1446 — adjacent, shouldn't conflict.
- **#1893 ↔ #1905:** different hunks of `manual_commit_push.go` (`prePush` vs `flushCheckpointRefsQueue`); clean.
- #1897 is merged; #1905's flipped tests are all single-remote, so #1893's gate doesn't touch them.

## Suggested order

**#1898 → #1905 → #1893.** #1898 is smallest and fixes a live misroute; #1905 rebases to drop the duplicate helper and fix two comments. #1893 goes last because it's the one that needs decisions: the tracking tier vs origin-only reads (item 2), the fork-guard hole it opens with #1898 (item 1), and merging its status line with #1905's note (item 4).

The one thing I'd block on is item 1 — it's a silent regression of a privacy guard, and it only becomes visible when you read the two PRs together.
